Touring Britain on an Electric Motorcycle in 2026: The Honest Truth

I've been riding electric motorcycles for touring over the past couple of years, and I'll be straight with you—it's completely changed how I plan my trips across Britain. Not always in the ways the manufacturers promise, either. By 2026, electric touring bikes have matured enough to be genuinely viable, but you need to approach route planning differently than you would on a petrol machine.

Let me share what I've learned from putting thousands of miles on electric tourers, from the sweeping curves of the NC500 to the twisty delights of the Welsh borders. This isn't marketing fluff—it's what actually works when you're out there with a charge meter instead of a fuel gauge.

The Reality of Electric Touring Range in 2026

First things first: forget what the spec sheet says about range. I've found that real-world touring range on most electric bikes sits around 60-70% of the quoted figure, especially when you're riding properly loaded with panniers and a top box fighting British headwinds.

My Energica Experia claims 260 miles. In reality, I plan for 160-180 miles between charges when touring, less if I'm tackling the Lake District or Scottish Highlands where you're constantly on the throttle climbing. The LiveWire Del Mar I tested last month quoted 150 miles but gave me a reliable 100-110 miles in typical touring conditions.

How Weather Affects Your Electric Range

British weather isn't kind to electric range. I've noticed around 20-25% range loss in cold, wet conditions compared to dry summer riding. That February trip to Scotland? Brutal on the battery. The bike's heating systems, your heated gear drawing power, cold batteries—it all adds up.

  • Cold weather (below 10°C): expect 20-30% range reduction
  • Heavy rain and headwinds: another 10-15% loss
  • Motorway speeds above 70mph: significantly worse efficiency than A-roads at 50-60mph
  • Mountain passes: the climbs hurt, but regenerative braking on descents claws some back

Planning Routes Around Charging Infrastructure

This is where touring electric differs massively from petrol touring. I now use VisorUp's route builder alongside charging apps like Zap-Map and PlugShare, and I plan my stops around rapid chargers rather than scenic layby lunch spots—though I try to combine both when possible.

By 2026, the charging network across Britain has improved dramatically. Most market towns now have at least one rapid charger, and popular touring routes have decent coverage. That said, I've learned some hard lessons about relying solely on apps.

Charging Network Realities

I've arrived at "available" chargers to find them occupied by cars (happens more often than you'd think), broken, or in pub car parks where you need to ask permission. Always have a backup charging location within range.

The A9 through the Highlands now has rapid chargers every 40-50 miles, which makes the run to Inverness perfectly manageable. The NC500, though? Still challenging. I completed it last summer, but it required careful planning and a couple of overnight hotel stops chosen specifically for their charging facilities.

Always arrive at your charging stop with at least 15-20% battery remaining. I've been caught out by broken chargers twice, and that buffer has saved me from a very expensive recovery truck ride.

Types of Chargers You'll Encounter

Understanding charger types has become as important as knowing your bike's fuel tank size used to be.

  • Rapid DC chargers (50kW+): These are your friends. 20-40 minutes for 80% charge on most touring bikes
  • Fast AC chargers (7-22kW): Useful for lunch stops or hotel overnight charging, but too slow for mid-route top-ups
  • Slow chargers (3kW): Basically useless for touring unless you're staying overnight

I carry adapters for Type 2 and CCS connectors, plus I've got a standard 3-pin plug adapter as an absolute emergency backup. Cost me £85 from SportsBikeShop, but it's pulled me out of trouble twice when rural chargers were down.

Best Electric Motorcycles for Touring in 2026

I've ridden most of the electric tourers available now, and there's a clear divide between bikes designed for touring versus those that can just about manage it.

Proper Electric Touring Bikes

The Energica Experia remains my top choice. Comfortable, genuinely capable of 150+ mile days, and the build quality handles British roads and weather brilliantly. I've taken mine through flooding on the Somerset Levels and across frost-damaged Scottish roads without issues.

Zero's SR/S has matured into a solid tourer too. Better range than earlier models, and the aftermarket luggage options have finally caught up. I prefer it for technical routes—that instant torque through the twisties around Snowdonia is addictive.

Bikes That Can Tour (With Compromises)

The LiveWire models are fantastic machines but the range makes multi-day tours stressful. I've used one for day trips out of Manchester and it's brilliant, but I wouldn't attempt the Island to Highlands route on one.

Practical Touring Tips for Electric Bikes

After two years of electric touring, these are the strategies that actually work for me on British roads.

Charging Strategy for Long Days

I've settled into a rhythm of charging to 80% rather than 100% during the day. That last 20% takes almost as long as the first 80%, and I'd rather be riding. I charge to 100% overnight when time isn't precious.

I plan my charging stops around rapid chargers near cafés or places I actually want to visit. That 30-minute charge stop at the services near Tebay? Perfect excuse to grab proper food rather than rushing through like I used to on petrol bikes.

Luggage and Weight Considerations

Electric bikes are already heavier than their petrol equivalents, so I've become ruthless about packing light. Check out the VisorUp packing checklist—I follow the lightweight touring approach and leave behind anything I "might" need rather than definitely will need.

Weight affects range more on electric bikes than petrol ones. I've measured around 8-10% range loss when fully loaded versus riding solo with minimal luggage.

Cold Weather Preparation

Battery performance drops in cold weather, so winter touring requires extra planning. I've learned to pre-heat the battery while still plugged in when possible—most bikes let you do this through the app now. Makes a noticeable difference to initial range.

I also ride in a lower power mode to extend range when it's cold. The instant torque means even Eco mode on most electric bikes is plenty quick enough for overtaking on A-roads.

Costs and Economics of Electric Touring

Let's talk money, because this is where electric touring gets interesting. My typical touring day covers 200-250 miles. On my old Tracer 900, that was £25-30 in fuel. On the Energica, it's £8-12 in charging costs, less if I can charge at hotels overnight on their standard rate.

However, the bikes cost more upfront. We're looking at £16,000-25,000 for a proper electric tourer versus £10,000-15,000 for an equivalent petrol sports tourer. The running costs are lower—no oil changes, fewer consumables, less maintenance—but it takes significant mileage to break even.

Hidden Costs to Consider

  • Charging network subscription fees (I use multiple networks, costs around £15/month total)
  • Accommodation with charging facilities often costs slightly more
  • Good charging cables and adapters (£150-200 for a complete kit)
  • Potentially higher insurance premiums, though this is improving

What Works Well About Electric Touring

Despite the challenges, I genuinely prefer electric touring now for certain types of trips. The forced stops every 120-150 miles mean I'm less fatigued—I used to push through on petrol bikes and arrive exhausted.

The smoothness is incredible for long days in the saddle. No vibration, no clutch hand fatigue, just effortless progress. That ride through the Yorkshire Dales last month was utterly sublime—floating through corners with instant, predictable power delivery.

Overnight costs can be lower too. I seek out hotels and B&Bs with charging, and many don't charge extra for it (though this might change as electric vehicles become more common). Some places actively advertise EV charging to attract guests.

Where Electric Touring Still Struggles

I won't pretend it's all perfect. Spontaneous route changes are more complicated—I can't just blast off down an interesting-looking lane without checking if it affects my charging strategy. That freedom to just ride is diminished.

Remote Scotland remains challenging. The charging infrastructure is improving, but there are still significant gaps. I attempted a tour of the Outer Hebrides and had to abandon it halfway through due to broken chargers and limited backup options.

Multi-day trips require more research and planning. I spend an hour planning electric touring routes that would take 15 minutes on a petrol bike. Some riders will find this annoying; I've learned to enjoy the anticipation.

My Electric Touring Essentials Checklist

Beyond the usual touring gear, these electric-specific items live permanently in my panniers:

  • Multiple charging network RFID cards (some chargers don't have app payment)
  • All possible adapter cables for different connector types
  • Portable battery pack to keep phone charged (essential when your phone is your charging map)
  • Physical backup list of charger locations along planned route
  • Membership to a motorcycle breakdown service that explicitly covers electric bikes
  • Insulated gloves for handling frozen charging cables in winter

The Future: 2026 and Beyond

The electric touring landscape is changing rapidly. Fast charging speeds are improving—some new bikes can charge at 100kW+, meaning 80% charge in under 20 minutes. Battery technology keeps advancing, with realistic 200+ mile touring ranges now available.

Infrastructure continues expanding too. Every month I notice new rapid chargers appearing in market towns that previously had nothing. The gap between petrol and electric touring convenience is narrowing, though it hasn't closed completely yet.

Is Electric Touring Right for You?

If you're considering making the switch, ask yourself honestly about your typical touring style. Do you ride structured routes or explore spontaneously? How remote do you typically go? Are you comfortable with technology and apps? How much patience do you have for charging stops?

For me, electric touring works brilliantly for planned multi-day tours across England, Wales, and southern Scotland. It's viable but challenging for the far north of Scotland. It's perfect for day tours and weekend trips within 300 miles of home.

I still keep a petrol bike for certain trips—the very remote stuff and ultra-long days where I want to cover 400+ miles. But 70% of my touring now happens on electric, and I genuinely prefer it for most situations.

Getting Started with Electric Touring

If you're ready to try electric touring, start with day trips from home. Find your local rapid chargers, practice using different networks, and get a feel for real-world range. Then build up to overnight trips before tackling week-long tours.

Use VisorUp's trip planner to map routes with charging stops included from the start—don't treat them as afterthoughts. Join electric motorcycle forums and Facebook groups; the community is incredibly helpful about sharing charging locations and route advice.

Consider test riding multiple electric bikes. They all have different characteristics, ranges, and charging speeds. What works for me might not suit your riding style or typical routes.

Electric motorcycle touring in 2026 isn't quite as convenient as petrol touring yet, but it's close enough that the benefits—lower costs, incredible smoothness, environmental advantages—make it genuinely worthwhile. I've learned to embrace the different rhythm of electric touring, and my riding has improved for it.

Start planning your first electric tour. Pick a route with good charging infrastructure, build in buffer time, and enjoy discovering a completely different way to experience Britain's incredible roads. See you out there—I'll be the one enjoying a coffee while the bike charges at Tebay.
